title: Review: Describing motion; Motion graphs; Constant-acceleration equations; Projectile motion; Friction; Drag and terminal velocity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: K03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; K02-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; K02-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; D11-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D05-1#N.11b, D11-1#N.14, K01-1#N.2, K03-1#N.16, D11-1#N.7, K01-1#N.10, K03-1#N.5a, D11-1#N.3, K01-1#N.5, K03-1#N.12. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Free fall
items.clue: Motion in which gravity is the only force acting on the object.

items.label: Acceleration
items.clue: Gradient of a velocity–time graph; uniform when the line is straight.

items.label: Distance
items.clue: Whole area on a velocity–time graph with every part counted as positive.

items.label: Drag
items.clue: Resistive force on an object moving through a fluid, increasing with speed.

questions.stem: A box sits on the flat floor of a van. The van speeds up forwards along a straight, level road, and the box does not slide on the floor. Which statement about the friction force on the box is correct?

options.text: It acts backwards, because friction always opposes the box's motion.
There is no friction force, because the box is not sliding on the floor.
It acts forwards, and it is the force that makes the box speed up.
It acts forwards, but an equal backward force balances it.

questions.explanation: The box speeds up with the van, so it needs a forward resultant force. The only horizontal force on it is friction from the floor, so friction acts forwards.

questions.stem: Two paper cones have the same size and shape. A second cone is pushed inside one of them, doubling its mass without changing its outside shape. Both are dropped from a high balcony. Which statement about their terminal velocities is correct?

options.text: Both reach the same terminal velocity, as all objects in free fall have the same acceleration.
The double cone reaches a higher terminal velocity, as drag must grow to equal a weight twice as large.
The double cone reaches a lower terminal velocity, as its greater weight gives it more drag at every speed.
The double cone reaches its terminal velocity sooner, as its greater weight gives it a greater acceleration from the start.

questions.stem: A runner moves along a straight track. Her position x is measured from a marker on the track. She starts at x = +30 m, runs to x = +70 m, then turns around and runs to x = −20 m, where she stops. What is her displacement?
A toy car is released from rest on a straight slope and speeds up with constant acceleration. It travels 0.60 m in the first 2.0 s. How far does it travel between t = 4.0 s and t = 6.0 s?
A ball is thrown at an angle in air. Its path comes down more steeply than it went up. What is the main reason?

options.text: Gravity pulls harder on the ball as it falls than as it rises, so it drops more steeply.
Drag keeps reducing the horizontal velocity, so it is smaller on the way down.
Drag acts only after the top of the path, when the ball's speed starts to increase again.
The ball loses all of its horizontal velocity at the top, so it falls almost straight down.

questions.explanation: Drag opposes the velocity for the whole flight, so the horizontal velocity falls all the time. Coming down, the ball covers less ground for each metre it falls: a steeper path.

questions.stem: A car travels 3.0 km along a straight road at a constant speed of 10 m s⁻¹, then returns along the same road to its starting point at a constant speed of 15 m s⁻¹. What are its average speed and its average velocity for the whole journey?

options.text: Average speed 12.5 m s⁻¹; average velocity 0 m s⁻¹
Average speed 12 m s⁻¹; average velocity 0 m s⁻¹
Average speed 12 m s⁻¹; average velocity 12 m s⁻¹
Average speed 12 m s⁻¹; average velocity −2.5 m s⁻¹

questions.stem: A car travelling at 16 m s⁻¹ brakes with uniform deceleration and comes to rest in 4.0 s. What distance does the car travel while braking?
A small steel ball is released from rest in air and falls until it reaches terminal velocity. How does its acceleration change during this time?

options.text: It is constant but less than g, because drag is constant.
It stays equal to g, since drag only lowers the ball's speed.
It increases, since the ball moves faster and faster as it falls.
It decreases from g towards zero as the drag increases.

questions.explanation: At release the ball is at rest, so there is no drag and its acceleration is g. As it speeds up the drag grows, so the acceleration decreases, reaching zero at terminal velocity.

questions.stem: An object moves along a straight line, with positive taken to the right. At one instant its velocity is −3.0 m s⁻¹ and its acceleration is +2.0 m s⁻². The acceleration stays constant. Which describes the motion of the object?

options.text: Moving left and slowing down; it will then stop and stay at rest.
Moving left and speeding up, since its acceleration is positive.
Moving left and slowing down; later it will move off to the right.
Moving right and speeding up, in the direction of its acceleration.

questions.stem: A student drops a ball from rest from several heights h and times each fall, t. She plots t² (y-axis) against h (x-axis): a straight line through the origin with gradient 0.204 s² m⁻¹. What value of g do the results give?
questions.explanation: h = ½gt² gives t² = (2/g)h, so the gradient is 2/g. g = 2 ÷ 0.204 = 9.80 m s⁻².
